def: Inflammation of the epiglottis, the cartilage flap over the airway, which can swell and obstruct breathing. Classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children, with drooling, muffled voice and a thumbprint sign on lateral neck x-ray.
A pus-filled cavity in lung tissue, usually after aspiration of oral bacteria or necrotizing pneumonia. Seen on imaging as a cavity with an air-fluid level, often in dependent segments.
A malignant tumor of the mesothelial cells lining the pleura (or peritoneum), strongly linked to asbestos exposure. Causes pleural thickening, effusion and chest pain, with a poor prognosis.
Inflammation of both the small intestine and the colon, producing diarrhea and abdominal pain. Examples include infectious forms and necrotizing enterocolitis of premature infants.
Large, heavily glycosylated proteins that make mucus gel and coat epithelial surfaces, protecting them from pathogens and injury. Secreted by goblet and other mucous cells.
Constriction of the pupil. Caused by parasympathetic stimulation, opioids, pilocarpine or loss of sympathetic input (as in Horner syndrome).

A band of white matter between the thalamus/caudate and the lentiform nucleus carrying motor and sensory fibers to and from the cortex. A small stroke here causes dense contralateral weakness (pure motor stroke).

A tripeptide antioxidant (glutamate, cysteine, glycine) that neutralizes reactive oxygen species and helps detoxify drugs. Regenerated by glutathione reductase using NADPH; depleted in acetaminophen overdose.
An alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the brainstem, lowering blood pressure. Also used for opioid withdrawal and ADHD; abrupt stopping can cause rebound hypertension.
The lymphoid tissue mass on each side of the back of the throat between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Part of Waldeyer ring; infected in tonsillitis, such as strep pharyngitis.

A malignancy of immature lymphoid precursor cells (lymphoblasts) that floods the marrow. Most common childhood cancer; TdT-positive blasts, associated with t(12;21) (good prognosis) and t(9;22) (poor).

Cranial nerve V, the main sensory nerve of the face and motor nerve of the muscles of mastication. Its three divisions are ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular; trigeminal neuralgia causes stabbing facial pain.

A benign tumor of Schwann cells, the myelin-forming cells of peripheral nerves, staining S-100 positive. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 2.
A paired venous channel on either side of the sella turcica that drains the face and orbit. Carries cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI and the internal carotid artery; infection can cause thrombosis.
A glial tumor arising from astrocytes, ranging from low-grade pilocytic tumors of children to aggressive glioblastoma. GFAP-positive; pilocytic types show Rosenthal fibers.
The main duct that carries pancreatic enzymes to the duodenum, usually joining the common bile duct at the major papilla. Obstruction by a stone or tumor can cause pancreatitis.
Protrusion of the soft nucleus pulposus through a tear in the annulus fibrosus, often compressing a nerve root. Most often at L4-L5 or L5-S1, causing sciatica or radiating arm pain.
A penicillinase-resistant penicillin used against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Given intravenously; adverse effects include interstitial nephritis.

Receptors that bind acetylcholine, divided into ligand-gated nicotinic channels and G protein-coupled muscarinic receptors. Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction are the target of antibodies in myasthenia gravis.
A yeast that normally colonizes mucosa and causes thrush, vaginitis and esophagitis, and invasive disease in immunocompromised patients. Forms pseudohyphae and germ tubes at 37 C.

The most common skin cancer, a slow-growing tumor of basal keratinocytes that rarely metastasizes. Pearly papule with telangiectasias and rolled borders, often on sun-exposed face; linked to hedgehog pathway mutations (PTCH1).
An aminoglycoside antibiotic that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and kills gram-negative bacteria. Causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
A gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe causing gas gangrene through alpha toxin (a lecithinase) and food poisoning from reheated meat. Produces double zones of hemolysis on blood agar.
Fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) that digest keratin and infect skin, hair and nails, causing tinea. Diagnosed by KOH prep showing hyphae.
A genus of obligate intracellular bacteria; Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, acquired by inhaling aerosols from livestock. Unlike other rickettsial diseases, it lacks a rash and is not vector-borne.
Inflammation of the vertebrae, as in ankylosing spondylitis or infectious (pyogenic or tuberculous) vertebral osteomyelitis. Causes back pain and stiffness.

An invasive infection by Mucor and Rhizopus molds with broad, nonseptate hyphae that branch at right angles. Causes rhinocerebral disease in diabetic ketoacidosis and neutropenic patients, with black necrotic tissue.

A group of disorders causing inflammation and scarring of the lung interstitium, leading to restrictive physiology and reduced diffusing capacity. Examples include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and sarcoidosis.
A thickened strip of ectoderm along the dorsal embryo that folds into the neural tube during the third and fourth weeks. Induced by the notochord; gives rise to the central nervous system.
The tough outer membrane covering the brain and spinal cord, with two layers that form the dural venous sinuses. Its folds include the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.
Rupture of the fetal membranes before labor begins and before 37 weeks of gestation. Raises the risk of chorioamnionitis and preterm delivery.

A common endocrine disorder with hyperandrogenism, irregular ovulation and polycystic-appearing ovaries, often with insulin resistance. Causes hirsutism, acne and infertility; treated with weight loss, OCPs and metformin.
A biguanide, first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, that lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity. Risk of lactic acidosis; does not cause hypoglycemia alone.
Scraping of tissue from a surface or cavity with a spoon-shaped instrument, such as dilation and curettage of the uterus. Used to obtain tissue or empty the uterus.
Severe peptic ulcer disease from a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) of the pancreas or duodenum, causing excess acid. Associated with MEN1 and diarrhea; diagnosed by high fasting gastrin.
The cartilage disc near the ends of long bones where lengthening occurs by endochondral ossification. Weakest point in a child's bone, so injuries here can disturb growth.
A hormone made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone, mediating most of its growth-promoting effects. Elevated in acromegaly and low in growth hormone deficiency.

An autoimmune destruction of the thyroid, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. Features anti-TPO and antithyroglobulin antibodies and lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and Hurthle cells.
An azole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis. Also inhibits human steroid synthesis, so it can cause gynecomastia and adrenal insufficiency.
The first intermediate of glucose metabolism, formed when hexokinase or glucokinase traps glucose in the cell. It feeds glycolysis, glycogen synthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway.
Reduced resistance to passive movement of a limb, giving a floppy feel. In infants it suggests lower motor neuron disease, myopathy or a genetic disorder such as Down or Prader-Willi syndrome.

Narrowing of the renal artery that reduces kidney perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin system, causing secondary hypertension. Caused by atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia; ACE inhibitors may worsen kidney function.
Abnormally low urine output, generally under 400 mL per day. Reflects prerenal, intrinsic renal or postrenal causes of kidney injury.
Ovarian follicle cells surrounding the granulosa cells that make androgens under LH stimulation. Granulosa cells convert these androgens to estrogen using aromatase.
A flat area of skin discoloration larger than a few millimeters caused by blood leaking into tissue, i.e. a bruise. Color changes from purple to green to yellow as hemoglobin breaks down.
The fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. By definition 100% for intravenous drugs; reduced by first-pass metabolism for oral drugs.

A genetic disease producing many fluid-filled cysts that enlarge the kidneys and destroy function. Autosomal dominant form (PKD1/PKD2) presents in adults with hypertension and berry aneurysms; recessive form presents in infancy.

The largest branch of the internal carotid artery, supplying the lateral cerebral cortex including face and arm motor and sensory areas. Occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness and aphasia or neglect.

An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome from TSC1 or TSC2 mutations causing hamartomas in many organs. Features include seizures, ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas, cardiac rhabdomyomas and renal angiomyolipomas.
A centrally acting alpha-2 agonist antihypertensive, a first-line drug for hypertension in pregnancy. Can cause positive Coombs test and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Inflammation or infection of colonic diverticula, small outpouchings of the bowel wall, typically the sigmoid colon. Causes left lower quadrant pain and fever; complications include abscess and perforation.

Inflammation of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses, causing congestion, facial pressure and discharge. Usually viral; bacterial cases involve Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
A cytokine made by Th17 cells that recruits neutrophils and promotes defense against fungi and extracellular bacteria. Drives psoriasis and spondyloarthritis; blocked by secukinumab.
Proteins whose blood levels rise (or fall) during inflammation, largely driven by IL-6 acting on the liver. Examples include CRP, fibrinogen and ferritin; albumin falls.
The active enzyme that breaks down fibrin clots, formed from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator. Inhibited by alpha-2 antiplasmin.
Obstruction of a blood vessel by a clot that formed elsewhere and traveled through the bloodstream. Deep vein thrombosis causing pulmonary embolism is the classic example.
A fourth-generation cephalosporin with activity against Pseudomonas and gram-positive organisms, given intravenously. Can cause neurotoxicity in kidney failure.
A short-acting beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, used for acute asthma and COPD. Side effects include tremor, tachycardia and hypokalemia.
Clear fluid made by the ciliary body that fills the front of the eye and nourishes the lens and cornea. Drains through the trabecular meshwork; impaired outflow raises eye pressure in glaucoma.
Inflammation of fascia, the connective tissue sheath around muscles. Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly spreading soft tissue infection with severe pain out of proportion to appearance.
Large circulating white blood cells with kidney-shaped nuclei that enter tissues and become macrophages. Phagocytose pathogens and present antigen.
A purine intermediate in the breakdown pathway: hypoxanthine is oxidized to xanthine and then to uric acid by xanthine oxidase. Blocked by allopurinol in gout.
Lymphocytes of the innate immune system that kill virus-infected and tumor cells lacking MHC class I, using perforin and granzymes. CD16 and CD56 positive.
A narrow channel in the midbrain linking the third and fourth ventricles. Stenosis blocks cerebrospinal fluid flow and causes hydrocephalus.

A lymphoid organ in the anterior mediastinum where T cells mature and undergo positive and negative selection. Develops from the third pharyngeal pouch; absent in DiGeorge syndrome and large in thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis.

The lateral part of the basal ganglia, forming the striatum with the caudate and part of the lentiform nucleus with the globus pallidus. Involved in motor control; affected in Huntington disease and Wilson disease.
A congenital abdominal wall defect, usually right of the umbilicus, in which bowel protrudes without a covering sac. Not typically associated with chromosomal abnormalities, unlike omphalocele.

An antiepileptic that blocks sodium channels, used for focal and generalized seizures and bipolar disorder. Can cause life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially with rapid titration or valproate.
A bacterial toxin chemically inactivated so it is harmless but still triggers antibody production. Used in tetanus and diphtheria vaccines.

Displacement of the femoral head from the femoral neck through the growth plate, typically in obese adolescents. Presents with hip or referred knee pain and limp; the head is posterior and inferior ("ice cream falling off cone").

Fungal infection from inhaling Histoplasma capsulatum spores, found in soil with bird or bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. Small intracellular yeast in macrophages; can mimic tuberculosis.
A genus of small gram-negative bacteria causing cat scratch disease (B. henselae), trench fever and bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients.
Inflammation of a bursa, the fluid-filled sac that cushions tendons and bones near joints. Causes local pain and swelling, such as in the shoulder, elbow or knee.
A CT scan with intravenous contrast timed to image blood vessels in detail. Used to diagnose pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection and aneurysms.
A genus of gram-positive rods that form club shapes and Chinese-letter arrangements. C. diphtheriae causes diphtheria via an exotoxin that inhibits elongation factor 2.
A genus of gram-negative rods in the gut flora; E. coli causes urinary tract infection, neonatal meningitis and traveler's diarrhea. Ferments lactose and appears pink on MacConkey agar.

A fungal pneumonia in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS and CD4 counts below 200. Presents with dry cough, hypoxia and ground-glass infiltrates; treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
The group B streptococcus, a gram-positive coccus that colonizes the vagina and causes neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis. Catalase negative, bacitracin resistant and CAMP test positive.
Guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that relay signals from cell-surface receptors to effector enzymes, switching on when bound to GTP. Types include Gs, Gi and Gq.
Drugs made from living cells, such as antibodies and fusion proteins, rather than chemical synthesis. Examples include TNF inhibitors like infliximab.
A weak androgen made by the adrenal cortex and gonads, converted to testosterone or estrone. Elevated in congenital adrenal hyperplasia and polycystic ovary syndrome.
A hormone released by duodenal S cells in response to acid that stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. Also slows gastric emptying.
Abnormally high blood phosphate, most often from kidney failure. Can cause secondary hyperparathyroidism and metastatic calcification.
Defective mineralization of bone matrix in adults, usually from vitamin D deficiency, causing soft, painful bones and fractures. The childhood equivalent is rickets.
A synthetic analog of vasopressin that acts on V2 receptors to concentrate urine. Used for central diabetes insipidus, bedwetting and von Willebrand disease or mild hemophilia A.
A cell-surface receptor that takes up LDL cholesterol from blood by endocytosis, mainly in the liver. Defective in familial hypercholesterolemia.
Testosterone-producing cells in the testicular interstitium between seminiferous tubules, stimulated by LH.
Supportive cells in the seminiferous tubules that nourish developing sperm, form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin and antimullerian hormone. Stimulated by FSH.
Pain or burning during urination, a typical symptom of urinary tract infection or urethritis.
Placenta that implants over or near the internal cervical os. Causes painless third-trimester vaginal bleeding; digital exam is avoided.
An abnormally high platelet count. Reactive causes include infection, iron deficiency and inflammation; primary causes include essential thrombocythemia.
A coagulation protein that acts as a cofactor for factor IXa in activating factor X. Deficient in hemophilia A, giving an elevated PTT with normal PT.
An oral glucocorticoid prodrug converted to prednisolone in the liver, used to suppress inflammation and immunity. Long-term use causes Cushingoid effects, osteoporosis and hyperglycemia.
A group of inherited diseases causing progressive muscle fiber degeneration and weakness. Duchenne type is X-linked, from dystrophin mutations, with Gowers sign and elevated creatine kinase.
An autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder from fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations. Causes tall stature, long fingers, lens dislocation upward, and aortic root dilation and dissection.
A stent placed through the liver connecting the portal vein to a hepatic vein to relieve portal hypertension. Used for variceal bleeding and refractory ascites; can cause hepatic encephalopathy.

Failure of the fetal ductus arteriosus connecting the aorta and pulmonary artery to close after birth. Causes a continuous machine-like murmur; associated with congenital rubella and treated with indomethacin.
White blood cells in the urine, indicating inflammation or infection of the urinary tract. Sterile pyuria suggests tuberculosis, chlamydia or interstitial nephritis.
A branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) that extends the elbow, wrist and fingers. Injury causes wrist drop, as in humeral shaft fracture.
Swelling of the optic disc due to raised intracranial pressure, seen on fundoscopy with blurred disc margins. Vision is usually preserved initially; enlarged blind spot.
A nitrate that releases nitric oxide to relax vascular smooth muscle, mainly dilating veins and reducing preload. Used for angina; headache and hypotension are side effects.

Serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists, such as sumatriptan, that constrict cranial blood vessels and block neuropeptide release. Used for acute migraine and cluster headache; contraindicated in coronary artery disease.
An antiplatelet prodrug that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Used after stent placement and acute coronary syndrome; activation depends on CYP2C19.

Chronic valve damage, especially mitral stenosis, from acute rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Caused by molecular mimicry between bacterial M protein and cardiac antigens; Aschoff bodies are characteristic.
Scarred, thickened, stiff pericardium that limits diastolic filling of the heart. Causes right-sided failure, a pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign; classic causes are tuberculosis and prior surgery.
A branch of the vagus nerve that supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Injury, such as during thyroidectomy, causes hoarseness; the left nerve loops under the aortic arch.
A nerve from C3-C5 that supplies motor innervation to the diaphragm. Irritation of the diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder; injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis.

Near-absence of immunoglobulins from failure of B cell development, as in X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia from a BTK mutation. Causes recurrent bacterial infections after maternal antibodies wane at about 6 months.
A secreted hepatitis B viral protein that marks active viral replication and high infectivity. Its disappearance and the appearance of anti-HBe signals reduced infectivity.
Rapid breathing in a term newborn from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, common after cesarean delivery. Chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures and streaky markings; usually resolves in days.
A protein stored in secretory granules of neuroendocrine cells, used as a tumor marker. Positive in pheochromocytoma, carcinoid and small cell lung cancer.
Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on one side of the face due to interrupted sympathetic supply to the eye. Caused by lesions such as Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection or brainstem stroke.
The activated form of coagulation factor X, which converts prothrombin to thrombin at the start of the common pathway. Inhibited by heparin (via antithrombin) and by rivaroxaban and apixaban.
Lipopolysaccharide from the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. Activates TLR4 to trigger cytokine release, fever and septic shock.
A fractionated heparin (e.g., enoxaparin) that mainly inhibits factor Xa via antithrombin. Has more predictable dosing and lower HIT risk than unfractionated heparin; cleared by the kidneys.
Pain felt in a part of the body distant from the true source because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord levels. For example, diaphragm irritation causes shoulder pain.
The plasma protein that carries iron in the blood. Increased in iron deficiency; decreased saturation distinguishes it from anemia of chronic disease.
Antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) that block breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. Can cause hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods and serotonin syndrome.
A benign, localized skin lesion composed of pigment cells, i.e. a mole, or other developmental malformation. Atypical or changing nevi may signal melanoma.
A genus of small gram-negative coccobacilli that infect the respiratory tract; B. pertussis causes whooping cough.
A gram-negative coccobacillus causing whooping cough with paroxysmal coughing and inspiratory whoop. Pertussis toxin raises cAMP by inhibiting Gi; lymphocytosis results.

A DNA virus causing recurrent cold sores (HSV-1) and genital lesions (HSV-2) and persisting latently in sensory ganglia. Causes temporal lobe encephalitis; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells.
A B cell lymphoma of lymph node follicles that is usually indolent. Caused by t(14;18) that overexpresses the antiapoptotic BCL2 protein.
A chronic inflammatory arthritis mainly affecting the sacroiliac joints and spine, leading to fusion ("bamboo spine"). HLA-B27-associated, with young men and morning stiffness; uveitis may occur.

An autoimmune blistering disease in older adults caused by IgG against hemidesmosomes (BP180) in the basement membrane. Gives tense subepidermal bullae with linear IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction; mucosa usually spared.
Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root from compression or inflammation, causing pain, numbness and weakness along its dermatome and myotome. Commonly from disc herniation.
A viral surface protein, notably on influenza, that binds sialic acid on host cells to initiate entry and agglutinates red cells. It is a major vaccine target and drives antigenic shift.
An antiviral guanosine analog activated by viral thymidine kinase (UL97), used for cytomegalovirus. Inhibits viral DNA polymerase; causes bone marrow suppression.

An intravenous or intramuscular beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits cell wall transpeptidases. Used for syphilis, streptococcal and meningococcal infection; destroyed by stomach acid and beta-lactamases.
A genus of curved, comma-shaped gram-negative rods that grow at 42 C. C. jejuni is a leading cause of bacterial diarrhea from poultry and can trigger Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Tissue-resident macrophages, particularly in connective tissue, that engulf debris and microbes. Proliferate in histiocytoses.
An antibiotic that blocks bacterial 50S peptidyl transferase. Causes dose-dependent anemia, aplastic anemia and gray baby syndrome in neonates.
Failure of the ovary to release an egg, a common cause of infertility and irregular or absent menses. Seen in polycystic ovary syndrome.
An atypical antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Can cause agranulocytosis (requiring blood count monitoring), seizures and myocarditis.
G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptors in parasympathetic target organs and the brain. M1, M3 and M5 act through Gq; M2 and M4 through Gi.

An inherited immunodeficiency from defective NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes cannot make a respiratory burst. Causes recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms; nitroblue tetrazolium or DHR test is abnormal.
A molecule that binds specifically to a receptor or other protein, such as a hormone binding its receptor.
The part of the forebrain that includes the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus. Relays sensory information and regulates homeostasis.

A clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells with BRAF mutations, causing bone lesions, skin rash and diabetes insipidus. Cells are S-100 and CD1a positive with Birbeck granules (tennis racket shape) on electron microscopy.
A group of disorders involving proliferation of histiocytes (macrophage and dendritic cells), such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
Membrane-bound sacs from the Golgi that store proteins and release them by exocytosis, often on a signal such as calcium.

Inability of the kidney to concentrate urine because collecting duct cells do not respond to ADH, causing large volumes of dilute urine. Caused by lithium, hypercalcemia or V2 receptor mutations; no response to desmopressin.
Non-enzymatic attachment of sugar to proteins or lipids, forming advanced glycation end products. Underlies HbA1c and contributes to diabetic complications.
A mitochondrial enzyme that breaks down monoamine neurotransmitters. MAO-A deaminates serotonin and norepinephrine; MAO-B mainly dopamine and is inhibited by selegiline.
A kidney tumor of young children arising from embryonic renal tissue (nephroblastoma). Presents as an abdominal mass; associated with WT1 deletion in WAGR syndrome and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
Infection of the uterine lining, most often after delivery, especially cesarean. Causes fever, uterine tenderness and foul lochia; polymicrobial, treated with clindamycin plus gentamicin.
The most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, an aggressive tumor of large B cells. Presents with a rapidly growing mass and is treated with R-CHOP.
The most common benign breast tumor in young women, a mobile, rubbery, painless mass. Composed of fibrous stroma and glandular tissue; may enlarge in pregnancy.
Small dilated blood vessels visible near the skin or mucosal surface. Seen in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, scleroderma (CREST) and ataxia-telangiectasia.
An autosomal recessive GAA trinucleotide repeat disorder in frataxin on chromosome 9, causing mitochondrial iron accumulation. Presents with ataxia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
Forced exhalation against a closed airway, which raises intrathoracic pressure and transiently lowers venous return. Used to terminate supraventricular tachycardia and to change murmur intensity.
A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries, linked to hepatitis B, with kidney, skin and nerve involvement but sparing the lungs. Angiography shows a "string of beads" with aneurysms.
Death of body tissue from lost blood supply or infection. Dry gangrene is ischemic and mummified; wet gangrene is infected; gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium.
Cellular injury when reactive oxygen species overwhelm antioxidant defenses, damaging lipids, proteins and DNA. Contributes to aging, ischemia-reperfusion injury and many diseases.
A sodium channel blocker used as a local anesthetic and class IB antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias. Toxicity causes CNS excitation and seizures.
A beta-1 selective blocker used for hypertension, angina, heart failure and arrhythmias. Side effects include bradycardia and fatigue; reduces mortality after myocardial infarction.
Viral inflammation of the larynx and trachea in young children, usually parainfluenza, causing a barking cough and stridor. Neck x-ray shows a steeple sign; treated with dexamethasone.

An enzyme that cleaves bonds by adding inorganic phosphate, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which releases glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen. Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase causes McArdle disease.
Epithelial cells lining the alveoli. Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface; type II cells secrete surfactant and regenerate the epithelium.
An enzyme that interconverts carbon dioxide and water with bicarbonate and a proton. Important in red cells, the kidney and the eye; inhibited by acetazolamide.
An anti-inflammatory cytokine made by Th2 cells and regulatory T cells that suppresses macrophage and Th1 activity.
A chemotherapy drug that causes DNA strand breaks through free radicals. Toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis; used in testicular cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma.
Nontuberculous mycobacteria that cause disseminated infection in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 50. Prophylaxed with azithromycin; also causes lung disease in older women.
